questions.q: In the older org-based development model (change sets), where does the "source of truth" for what a Flow or Permission Set actually contains live?
options: Inside the org itself
In a local JSON file tracked in Git
In the Metadata API's package.xml manifest
In the Salesforce CLI's local cache
questions.explain: Under org-based development, the org itself is the source of truth — there's no local, version-controlled file describing the metadata until Salesforce DX introduces source-driven development.

questions.q: What is the central shift that Salesforce DX's source-driven development model makes compared to org-based development?
options: It removes the need for a Dev Hub
It replaces Apex with a new programming language
A local, version-controlled set of files becomes the source of truth, and orgs become places that source is deployed to and synced from
It eliminates the need for sandboxes entirely
questions.explain: Source-driven development makes the local project (tracked in Git) the authoritative source of truth; orgs — including scratch orgs — become disposable targets that the source gets deployed to and synced from.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the five pieces of the Salesforce DX toolchain described in this lesson?
options: Change sets
The Developer Console
Classic Setup menus
Scratch orgs
questions.explain: Scratch orgs — disposable, short-lived orgs created on demand from a Dev Hub — are one of the five core pieces, alongside the Salesforce CLI, a standard project structure, the Metadata API in source format, and packaging.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce DX break Metadata API components into individual readable files (source format) instead of one opaque bundle?
options: To make the files smaller for faster upload speeds only
So that a diff in version control (like Git) actually shows what changed, enabling code review and history
Because the Metadata API no longer supports bundled formats
To remove the need for a package.xml manifest entirely
questions.explain: Readable, individual source-format files make Git diffs meaningful — you can see exactly what changed in a Flow or Apex class, review it, and track its history, which an opaque bundle doesn't support.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the relationship between knowing Apex/Flow/the data model and knowing Salesforce DX?
options: Salesforce DX is the operational layer underneath that work, comparable to Git and a build pipeline for an application developer
Salesforce DX replaces the need to know Apex or Flow
They are entirely unrelated skill sets with no connection
Salesforce DX is only relevant to Salesforce admins, never developers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly compares Salesforce DX to Git and a build pipeline sitting underneath an application developer's code — it's the operational layer, not a replacement for platform knowledge like Apex, Flow, or data modeling.
